text:
This paper explores sentence-level classification tasks using convolutional neural networks trained on top of pre-trained word vectors [P1_p1_c02]. Word vectors project words from a sparse, 1-of-V encoding onto a lower-dimensional vector space, acting as feature extractors that encode semantic features [P1_p1_c03]. 

The main idea is a simple convolutional neural network architecture [P1_p1_c02, P1_p5_c04]. Let a sentence of length $n$ be represented as $x_{1:n} = x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus \dots \oplus x_n$, where $\oplus$ is the concatenation operator [P1_p2_c01]. A convolution operation applies a filter $w \in \mathbb{R}^{hk}$ to a window of $h$ words to produce a new feature $c_i = f(w \cdot x_{i:i+h-1} + b)$, with a bias term $b \in \mathbb{R}$ and a non-linear function $f$ [P1_p2_c01]. This filter is applied to each possible word window to produce a feature map $c = [c_1, c_2, \dots, c_{n-h+1}]$ [P1_p2_c01]. Next, a max-over-time pooling operation takes the maximum value $\hat{c} = \max\{c\}$ as the feature for that filter, which naturally handles variable sentence lengths [P1_p2_c01]. Multiple filters with varying window sizes extract multiple features that form the penultimate layer, feeding into a fully connected softmax layer for label probabilities [P1_p2_c02]. A multichannel architecture uses one static channel and one fine-tuned channel [P1_p2_c02].

Key results show that a baseline model with randomly initialized words (CNN-rand) performs poorly, but static pre-trained vectors (CNN-static) achieve remarkable performance, competing with complex deep learning models [P1_p4_c03]. Fine-tuning gives further improvements (CNN-non-static) [P1_p4_c03]. Overall, the models improve upon the state of the art on 4 out of 7 tasks [P1_p1_c02].
